title: Infra: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts, networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD, and runbooks — consolidated playbook (2028 addendum)
author: Priya Malhotra
content:
Summary

This consolidated playbook describes Redwood's current recommended practices for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud account and networking hygiene, Terraform/IaC module usage, CI/CD for infra changes, and operational runbooks. It aggregates decisions and operational procedures from team wikis and runbooks (2024–2026) into a single reference for on-call engineers, infra owners, and SREs.

Scope

- All GPU-serving clusters (hosted, dedicated pools, private deployments) managed by eng-infra.
- All Terraform and CI/CD workflows that provision GPU instances, networking, and associated IAM.
- Runbooks covering capacity incidents, node replacement, and network failover.

Goals and measurable SLOs

- Average GPU cluster utilization target (steady-state): 55–70% to maintain headroom for bursty traffic.
- Provisioning lead time SLA for planned capacity: <= 7 calendar days for cloud accounts with pre-approved quotas; <= 14 days for accounts requiring quota requests.
- Node replacement RTO (from alert to healthy nodes): 20 minutes for a single-node failure, 60 minutes for multi-node incidents.
- Terraform drift detection: daily scan with anomalies auto-opened as issues.

High-level architecture and ownership

- GPU Fleet: k8s nodepools (GKE/EKS) for hosted and dedicated deployments; on-prem clusters use identical IaC modules but different provisioning runners. Owner: infra-gpu-team (eng-infra).
- Cloud Accounts and Networking: centralized org accounts managed by infra-cloud team; per-customer accounts for private deployments. Owner: infra-cloud.
- Terraform/IaC modules: maintained in repo infra/terraform-modules. Owners: infra-iac-team.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions + Atlantis for PR-driven changes; production applies gated by runbook approvals. Owners: infra-ci-team.

Capacity planning model (how we size and add capacity)

1) Inputs
   - 7-day and 90-day QPS/RTT trends for token throughput by model family.
   - Token-per-second performance curves per GPU type (A100, H100, L4) from benchmarking suite.
   - Peak concurrency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) and burst multipliers by customer tier.

2) Headroom policy
   - Maintain 30% headroom above forecasted p95 demand for regional pools.
   - Maintain a minimum of 2 spare nodes per nodepool for fast replacement.

3) Scaling cadence
   - Autoscale: short-term bursts handled by autoscaler with max surge 20% of nodepool.
   - Planned additions: submit capacity request ticket when sustained usage > 65% for 72 hours.
   - Emergency procurement: follow the emergency procurement runbook (see Runbooks section).

Cloud accounts and networking standards

- Account naming: rwd-{env}-{region}-{purpose} (e.g., rwd-prod-us-west-2-gpu).
- VPC design: 3-tier subnet layout (private worker subnets, private control-plane subnets, shared services subnet).
- Networking rules: GPU worker subnets are private, require NAT for outbound egress; control-plane and CI/CD runners have restricted egress via proxy.
- Peerings and endpoints: use AWS PrivateLink or equivalent for service endpoints (S3, ECR, Secrets Manager); avoid internet-facing control plane endpoints.
- Security groups / NSGs: lock down SSH/RDP to bastion subnets; allow only required inter-service ports (gRPC 9000–9100, metrics 9090, health-checks).
- IP allocation: reserve /20 per region for GPU workloads to allow growth.

Terraform / IaC module guidelines

- Module repo: github.com/redwood/infra/terraform-modules. Primary modules:
  - module/gpu-cluster (creates nodepool, autoscaler, node labels, taints)
  - module/networking-vpc (VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT gateways)
  - module/iam (roles, instance profiles, service accounts)
  - module/ami-bake (image pipeline hooks)
  - module/k8s-bootstrap (bootstrap K8s components, node labels/taints)

- Versioning: tag modules with semver. Consumers must pin module versions in root module (no floating master).
- Workspaces: one workspace per account/region combination. Use consistent naming: {env}-{region}-{logical-stack}.
- State backend: Terraform Cloud or S3 with DynamoDB locking (depending on account). Ensure encryption at rest and restricted access to state buckets.
- Secrets: never store secrets in tfvars; use Vault or cloud-native secrets and reference via providers at apply time.

CI/CD and build pipeline standards

- Repo layout: infra/terraform (root stacks), infra/modules (reusable modules), infra/packer (AMI recipes), infra/images (container build configs).
- PR policy: all Terraform changes require a PR with plan output and one approver from infra-iac-team + owner of affected module.
- Pipeline steps (GitHub Actions + Atlantis):
  1. lint (tflint, checkov),
  2. terraform validate,
  3. terraform plan (against isolated workspace),
  4. automated tests (unit tests for modules via kitchen-terraform or terratest),
  5. manual approval for apply to prod.
- Apply mechanism: Atlantis for non-prod automatic applies; production applies require manual runbook confirmation (see Production Apply checklist).
- Image build and signing: AMIs built in infra/packer pipeline, scanned with Trivy, signed and published to account-specific image registry. Container images go through the same vulnerability scan and are signed.

Production Apply checklist (manual gate)

1) Ensure on-call engineer is paged and available.
2) Confirm ticket exists and capacity justification is documented.
3) Verify terraform plan diffs and ensure no unexpected IAM or network changes.
4) Confirm backups: DB snapshots (if any), state snapshot exported to secure storage.
5) Run apply during approved maintenance window or with explicit approval in the ticket.

Runbooks (most critical)

A. GPU node eviction (OOM / GPU driver crash) — immediate steps
1. Pager alert triggers: alert includes node name, GPU type, pod list.
2. SSH to bastion and kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep <node>.
3. kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force.
4. Confirm pods rescheduled; if pods fail due to scheduling constraints, increase nodepool temporarily with:
   - Terraform: terraform workspace select {ws}; terraform apply -var 'node_count+=1' -target=module.gpu-cluster.nodepool (follow module-specific var names).
5. Replace node: terminate instance from cloud console (autoscaler will create a new one) or run node replacement job in buildkite/GHA.
6. If driver issue: run gpu-driver-reinstall script from /opt/bin on node image or promote new AMI after quick bake.
7. Post-incident: record metrics, tag incident, open follow-up doc.

B. Node pool scaling failure (quota/limit error)

1. Check cloud provider quota for GPUs in the account: AWS console -> Limits -> EC2 GPU instances.
2. If quota exhausted, trigger quota request playbook: open ticket with cloud provider, follow backoff mitigation (shift load to other regions, use alternate GPU type via routing policy).
3. For immediate mitigation, use smaller GPUs (e.g., L4) for lower-criticality workloads by updating routing tags.

C. Network partition / VPC connectivity loss

1. Verify control-plane reachability (SSM, Bastion).
2. If VPC route tables corrupted: roll back last terraform apply on networking-vpc workspace.
3. If peering flaps: failover to secondary region (traffic router policy) and notify routing owner.

Daily/Weekly operational checks

- Daily: verify cluster autoscaler status, node health, and drift scan results.
- Weekly: capacity report (per-region GPU utilization, queued requests), open capacity requests if trending upward.
- Monthly: module dependency updates (bump provider versions in a controlled PR and test in non-prod).

Incident postmortem expectations

- Every incident that exceeds SLOs must have a postmortem within 3 business days. Postmortem must include timeline, root cause, mitigation, and ownership for fixes. Link to central postmortem template in oncall-and-incident-response.

Operational tooling and logs

- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for metrics ingestion; dashboards for GPU utilization, pod scheduling failures, and network errors.
- Traces: Jaeger for control plane operations.
- Logs: aggregated to Loki/Elastic; index GPU driver logs for easier triage.
- Alerts: critical alerts page to on-call rotation; non-critical go to infra-signal channel.

Ownership, escalation, and contacts

- Primary owners: infra-gpu-team (pager), infra-iac-team (PR approvals), infra-cloud (quota and networking), infra-ci-team (pipeline issues).
- Escalation matrix:
  1. Primary on-call (15 minutes),
  2. Team lead (30 minutes),
  3. Eng SRE manager (60 minutes),
  4. CTO escalation if > 4 hours impact to production.

Appendices

A. Example Terraform commands
   - terraform workspace select prod-us-west-2-gpu
   - terraform plan -var-file=prod-us-west-2.tfvars -out=plan.out
   - terraform apply plan.out

B. Example GitHub Actions snippet (apply gate)
   - name: Terraform Apply Gate
     if: github.event.pull_request.merged && contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'production')
     run: |
       ./scripts/confirm-production-apply.sh

C. Useful links
   - infra/terraform-modules repo: https://github.com/redwood/infra/terraform-modules
   - Runbooks collection: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/
   - Capacity dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/infra/gpu-capacity

Change log (summary)

- 2024-11-15: Initial consolidated playbook (Priya Malhotra).
- 2025-06-02: Added production apply checklist and image signing notes (Ethan Chen).
- 2026-12-01: Addendum covering autoscaler surge policy and workspace naming conventions; updated SLOs (María González).

If you are executing a production change, follow the Production Apply checklist and notify the infra-oncall channel before starting. For any questions about ownership or gaps in this playbook, ping infra-team@redwood.internal.
